## CI: AI supply-chain review of action bumps

`.github/workflows/action-bump-review.yaml` has a read-only Copilot agent
(`.github/agents/action-supply-chain-review.md`, pinned model, strict JSON verdict) assess the upstream diff of every
digest bump on `renovate/*` PRs – except bumps of the popular actions that gate on Renovate's minimum release age
instead (`.github/renovate.json`'s release-age rule: GitHub's `actions/*` and `jdx/mise-action`) – and post the verdict
as a PR comment; the job's conclusion is the check a later automerge policy gates on (shadow phase until then). The
Copilot CLI comes from mise (`[tools] copilot`, backend `aqua:github/copilot-cli`, pinned in `mise.lock`) – the mise
manager bumps it and the minor/patch automerge rule merges it like any other repo tool. Facts below verified against
Copilot CLI 1.0.112 (2026-11-16); CLI flags: [programmatic
reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-programmatic-reference), [billing in
Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-cli/copilot-cli-in-github-actions).

- Auth env precedence is `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` > `GH_TOKEN` > `GITHUB_TOKEN` > stored login: a `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the
  environment that lacks the Copilot Requests permission silently shadows an existing login and fails auth. CI relies on
  this order – passing the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` bills Copilot CLI usage to the repository owner's Copilot seat on
  personally-owned repositories (no PAT needed).
- In `-p` runs every tool request that would prompt is denied. Exception: shell commands the CLI classifies as read-only
  run *without asking* – so `--deny-tool shell` (deny rules beat every allow rule and mode) is what actually closes the
  shell surface for the reviewer agent, alongside `--deny-tool write`, `--deny-tool memory`, `--disable-builtin-mcps`
  and `--disallow-temp-dir`.
- `--max-ai-credits` hard-caps a session's spend; its minimum is 30.
- `--usage-output-file` writes final usage JSON (`totalPremiumRequestCost`, `providerModelMetrics[].usage` with token
  classes) – the workflow includes it in the PR comment for cost calibration.
- Repository-level custom agents (`.github/agents/<id>.md`, id = file name without extension) are only discovered in
  prompt mode with `--trust-folder`.
- `--reasoning-effort` accepts none/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh/max; Claude Sonnet 5.5 accepts `high`
  (smoke-verified).
- The compare API omits `files[].patch` for binary or oversized files (source: [compare
  commits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/compare-two-commits)): files without a trusted-side reconstruction
  are surfaced as explicit unreviewable notes and the agent's verdict rules fail closed on them.
- The reviewer input file is capped at 500000 bytes (`.github/scripts/review_input.py enrich` assembles it): the diff
  comes first and one that does not fit is truncated with an explicit marker, which the agent must treat as
  unreviewable; context sections (upstream commits with authorship and signature state, tag/release context with release
  notes, BASE-revision workflow files referencing the action, the PR description) are appended in that priority order
  only while the budget has room – an omitted section leaves a one-line note in the file.
- Files whose patch the compare API omitted get their diffs reconstructed trusted-side: the workflow fetches the old and
  new git blobs (one `git/trees/{old}?recursive=1` call maps the old-side blob SHAs; `files[].sha` is the new side's)
  and `review_input.py` inserts capped unified diffs into the diff phase – per-file cap 128 KiB with an explicit
  truncation marker, NUL-sniff binary detection, `*.map` skipped as derivative of the `src/` patches, at most 4 files.
  Verified against tj-actions/changed-files v47.0.1→v47.0.2 (the dist bundle reconstructs to ~107 KiB across 97 hunks –
  fits the budget) and nick-fields/retry v2.9.0→v3.0.0 (~1 MiB – truncates at the cap), 2026-11-17.
- Digest-to-tag matching uses `repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags?per_page=100`; its `commit.sha` is the commit the tag points
  to, so annotated tags match too (verified for both tag styles against jdx/mise-action and git/git v2.44.0, 2026-11-16;
  source: [list repository tags](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos#list-repository-tags)).
- Renovate's github-actions manager rewrites a digest bump together with the pin's trailing `# vX.Y.Z` version comment
  and touches nothing else in the file (verified on PR #29's diff, Renovate 44, 2026-11-16). The review workflow's
  tamper guard normalizes a pin whose ref is exactly a digest followed only by whitespace or the version comment on that
  basis: digest+comment rewrites of any pin pass, any other edit to the workflow – including a longer or floating ref –
  trips.

Two matchStrings because each import line carries the version twice (path segment and hk@X# marker) and both occurrences must be rewritten – the same invariant bump-hk.sh enforces for manual bumps. The CI check catches partial desyncs regardless: mise install --locked errors when mise.toml and mise.lock disagree.",
      "managerFilePatterns": [
        "/^hk\\.pkl$/"
      ],
      "matchStrings": [
        "download/v(?<currentValue>\\d+\\.\\d+\\.\\d+)/hk",

The changelog entry for the bumped version is filled post-merge by the apk-bump workflow (CI; the hosted Renovate app cannot run post-upgrade tasks). Merge behavior and grouping are decided per update type by the chained apk rules below – see the repository-root KNOWLEDGE.md apk package version policy.",

## CI: Branch protection and platform-native automerge

`main` is branch-protected with required status checks (no review requirement, admin bypass on). Dependency-bump PRs
merge via GitHub's **native auto-merge**: `.github/renovate.json` sets `platformAutomerge: true`, the repository setting
"Allow auto-merge" is on. Renovate enables auto-merge on the PR and GitHub merges it the moment every required check is
green on the PR head – merging does not wait for the hosted Renovate app's run cadence. The required checks are the
*only* merge gate in this configuration – with none set, GitHub merges auto-merge PRs without waiting for CI (GitHub
docs' own warning) – so the required set below must stay in sync with the workflows: renaming a job, adding an app (its
`Lint app <name>` leg), or dropping a check needs the same change in the protection rule.

Required set (contexts are the job `name:` strings):

- `Find apps`, `Mise check (lint + validate)`, `Device-visible app changes require a version bump`, `Initialize builds`,
  `Build gate` – unconditional on every PR. `Build gate` (builder.yaml) folds the conditional `Build <app>` matrix into
  one static context: required checks must report on every PR, the matrix only runs when init finds changed app files,
  and the multi-arch build is a real gate for apk-pin PRs – the per-arch Alpine index race can fail one arch while the
  other passes (§"apk package version policy"). It passes on `skipped`, fails on any other non-success matrix result.
- `Lint app hd-idle`, `Lint app hickory-dns`, `Lint app nfs-server` – the find-addons matrix is repo-static (three
  apps).
- Deliberately not required: `Action supply-chain review (shadow)` (path-filtered, shadow phase – see §"CI: AI
  supply-chain review of action bumps"), `Build <app>` (dynamic matrix names; skipped legs never report), the
  apk-bump/publish-reconcile/skills-update workflows (post-merge or scheduled only).

Protection specifics: `strict: false` – no "require branches up to date". With it on, every merge invalidates every
other in-flight PR, and each invalidation becomes a rebase plus a fresh CI cycle; without it, a PR's CI certifies its
head against the `main` of that moment and the merge lands on a newer tip. Accepted trade for dependency bumps:
file-disjoint updates re-validated against a slightly newer tip add no signal (per-dep rationale in renovate.json's rule
descriptions). `required_linear_history: true` keeps the `automergeStrategy: rebase` property (one conventional commit
per bump, no merge bubbles; GitHub replays the branch's single commit onto the tip at merge time).
`rebaseWhen: conflicted` keeps Renovate from force-push-rebasing behind-but-clean branches: green check runs stay
attached to the unchanged head, so a batch opens in one window and drains in parallel – the apk-bump nudge's explicit
`@renovate rebase` comments still force rebase when the Alpine index race requires fresh runs.

Schedules: `after 8pm on sunday` + `before 8am on monday` (12 h strip, Europe/Zurich, all managers incl. apk). The
hosted app's runs are irregular and `updateNotScheduled` (default `true`) suppresses branch/PR creation outside the
window, so a missed run pushes a whole week's bumps out by a week. Batch intent: PRs open Sunday evening, required
checks run in parallel, everything eligible is merged before Monday 8am. `automergeSchedule` stays unset ("at any
time"): a batch whose CI finishes after 8am should still land instead of waiting a week. When changing this setup, apply
the protection rule (and "Allow auto-merge") *before* flipping `platformAutomerge` on: with the config live first,
GitHub merges auto-merge-enabled PRs while the required contexts don't exist yet, and heads that predate a newly
required context can never report it – they must be merged or rebased before the rule applies.

## CI: AI supply-chain review of action bumps

`.github/workflows/action-bump-review.yaml` has a read-only Copilot agent
(`.github/agents/action-supply-chain-review.md`, pinned model, strict JSON verdict) assess the upstream diff of every
digest bump on `renovate/*` PRs – except bumps of the popular actions that gate on Renovate's minimum release age
instead (`.github/renovate.json`'s release-age rule: GitHub's `actions/*` and `jdx/mise-action`) – and post the verdict
as a PR comment; the job's conclusion is the check a later automerge policy gates on (shadow phase until then). The
Copilot CLI comes from mise (`[tools] copilot`, backend `aqua:github/copilot-cli`, pinned in `mise.lock`) – the mise
manager bumps it and the minor/patch automerge rule merges it like any other repo tool. Facts below verified against
Copilot CLI 1.0.112 (2026-11-16); CLI flags: [programmatic
reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-programmatic-reference), [billing in
Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-cli/copilot-cli-in-github-actions).

- Auth env precedence is `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` > `GH_TOKEN` > `GITHUB_TOKEN` > stored login: a `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the
  environment that lacks the Copilot Requests permission silently shadows an existing login and fails auth. CI relies on
  this order – passing the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` bills Copilot CLI usage to the repository owner's Copilot seat on
  personally-owned repositories (no PAT needed).
- In `-p` runs every tool request that would prompt is denied. Exception: shell commands the CLI classifies as read-only
  run *without asking* – so `--deny-tool shell` (deny rules beat every allow rule and mode) is what actually closes the
  shell surface for the reviewer agent, alongside `--deny-tool write`, `--deny-tool memory`, `--disable-builtin-mcps`
  and `--disallow-temp-dir`.
- `--max-ai-credits` hard-caps a session's spend; its minimum is 30.
- `--usage-output-file` writes final usage JSON (`totalPremiumRequestCost`, `providerModelMetrics[].usage` with token
  classes) – the workflow includes it in the PR comment for cost calibration.
- Repository-level custom agents (`.github/agents/<id>.md`, id = file name without extension) are only discovered in
  prompt mode with `--trust-folder`.
- `--reasoning-effort` accepts none/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh/max; Claude Sonnet 5.5 accepts `high`
  (smoke-verified).
- The compare API omits `files[].patch` for binary or oversized files (source: [compare
  commits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/compare-two-commits)): files without a trusted-side reconstruction
  are surfaced as explicit unreviewable notes and the agent's verdict rules fail closed on them.
- The reviewer input file is capped at 500000 bytes (`.github/scripts/review_input.py enrich` assembles it): the diff
  comes first and one that does not fit is truncated with an explicit marker, which the agent must treat as
  unreviewable; context sections (upstream commits with authorship and signature state, tag/release context with release
  notes, BASE-revision workflow files referencing the action, the PR description) are appended in that priority order
  only while the budget has room – an omitted section leaves a one-line note in the file.
- Files whose patch the compare API omitted get their diffs reconstructed trusted-side: the workflow fetches the old and
  new git blobs (one `git/trees/{old}?recursive=1` call maps the old-side blob SHAs; `files[].sha` is the new side's)
  and `review_input.py` inserts capped unified diffs into the diff phase – per-file cap 128 KiB with an explicit
  truncation marker, NUL-sniff binary detection, `*.map` skipped as derivative of the `src/` patches, at most 4 files.
  Verified against tj-actions/changed-files v47.0.1→v47.0.2 (the dist bundle reconstructs to ~107 KiB across 97 hunks –
  fits the budget) and nick-fields/retry v2.9.0→v3.0.0 (~1 MiB – truncates at the cap), 2026-11-17.
- Digest-to-tag matching uses `repos/{owner}/{repo}/tags?per_page=100`; its `commit.sha` is the commit the tag points
  to, so annotated tags match too (verified for both tag styles against jdx/mise-action and git/git v2.44.0, 2026-11-16;
  source: [list repository tags](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos#list-repository-tags)).
- Renovate's github-actions manager rewrites a digest bump together with the pin's trailing `# vX.Y.Z` version comment
  and touches nothing else in the file (verified on PR #29's diff, Renovate 44, 2026-11-16). The review workflow's
  tamper guard normalizes a pin whose ref is exactly a digest followed only by whitespace or the version comment on that
  basis: digest+comment rewrites of any pin pass, any other edit to the workflow – including a longer or floating ref –
  trips.

# TODOs

Cross-app work items (tooling, CI, harnesses); app-specific items live in each app's `TODO.md`. Underlying technical
facts live in the repository-root `KNOWLEDGE.md`; procedures in the skills under `.agents/skills/`.

## Tasks

- Flip the AI supply-chain review from shadow to gating (skill/citation: root `KNOWLEDGE.md` §"CI: AI supply-chain
  review of action bumps", §"CI: Branch protection and platform-native automerge"): once
  `.github/workflows/action-bump-review.yaml` verdicts have been validated over a few real Renovate action bumps
  (`.github/renovate.json` package rules), make the review check a required context and set `automerge: true`
  (minor/patch, rebase strategy) for `tj-actions/changed-files` and `nick-fields/retry`. Under platform-native automerge
  the merge gate is the branch protection required-check set alone – the review job's conclusion blocks a merge only as
  a required context, and required contexts must report on every PR, so the flip needs the review job to run-and-report
  unconditionally (internal no-op skip for PRs without a reviewable action bump) instead of its current `paths:` filter.
  Preconditions: the review job's hardening fixes are on `main` (fork pull requests skipped; the tamper guard covers the
  verdict scripts and the mise toolset) and a dispatch run has exercised the pipeline end-to-end. Digest-typed updates
  (a ref repointed without a release) stay manual regardless: release-age gates cannot soak them (github-tags timestamps
  age against the original release) and they are the highest-signal event for human review.

- Upstream: file an hk issue/PR against [jdx/hk](https://github.com/jdx/hk) – its shebang-based file typing (v2.7.0,
  `src/file_type.rs`) does not recognize `#!/usr/bin/with-contenv bashio` (the Home Assistant base image's interpreter
  for s6-overlay scripts): wrapper interpreter plus unknown `bashio` argument resolve to plain text, so hk's
  shellcheck/shfmt/shellharden builtins (types `sh`/`bash`) silently skip every app script. Desired: look through
  s6-overlay's `with-contenv` (and similar env-style wrappers) to the real interpreter and type `bashio` as shell – the
  file content is plain bash. Until then, `hk.pkl` re-declares each shell builtin's `match_any` with added glob
  selectors for the s6 script paths (see the `s6Globs` comment there); the glob additions can be dropped once this
  lands. All three shell steps also cover the apps' `/usr/bin` scripts via the `appBinGlobs` selector.

- Upstream: file an hk issue against [jdx/hk](https://github.com/jdx/hk) (likely co-filed with
  [owenlamont/ryl](https://github.com/owenlamont/ryl)) – the `ryl` builtin's fix-mode wiring silently passes files with
  unfixable violations. hk's fix mode runs `check_diff` first and skips the fixer when it exits 0; ryl 0.26.0's `--diff`
  exit code reflects only patch presence: it exits 0 whenever nothing is fixable – including files carrying unfixable
  warnings or errors (probed 2026-10-20: `ryl check --diff` on a duplicate-key error file exits 0, and `--strict` does
  not change `--diff` exit codes; a fixable brace-spacing file prints the patch and exits 1). With the builtin as
  shipped (hk v2.7.0 `pkl/builtins/ryl.pkl`: `check_diff = ryl check --diff {{files}}`, `check_after_diff = true`),
  every pre-commit run (fix mode) passes files that `hk check --all` fails – the `check_after_diff` recheck never fires
  because no diff was applied. hk's own builtin test misses this: `testMaker.fixFail` exercises the fix command
  directly, not the check_diff-first flow the hook actually takes. Investigate which side should own the fix: ryl
  exiting non-zero from `--diff` when diagnostics exist without fixes, or hk not treating `check_diff` exit 0 as "clean"
  for partial fixers (e.g. re-running `check` when the fixer is skipped). Until then, this repo's `hk.pkl` clears
  `check_diff`/`check_after_diff`/`check_list_files` on the ryl step and puts `--strict` on both `check` and `fix` (the
  fix run is self-verifying: exit 0 only when nothing remains to fix or flag); the overrides can be dropped once this
  lands.

- Upstream: file an issue against [owenlamont/ryl](https://github.com/owenlamont/ryl) asking for a way to silence the
  summary that `ryl format --check`/`--diff` unconditionally end with on stderr (`N files already formatted`; the
  formatter docs record it as designed). Probed 2026-11-14 on 0.29.0: no CLI flag silences it (`--check` has no
  `--quiet`; `--output-format` styles findings but the summary ignores the format selection) and `[output]` can route a
  whole format's rendering elsewhere but not drop the summary. No existing issue found searching `quiet`/`summary` the
  same day. The tombi/ruff hk builtins pass `--quiet` and are silent; this repo's workaround (hk `ryl-format` step): the
  check routes its diff preview to stdout via `--config-data 'output = { standard = { path = "-" } }'` and drops stderr,
  keeping failures verbose. The routing and stderr drop can be replaced by the flag once it lands.

- Upstream: file an issue against [owenlamont/ryl](https://github.com/owenlamont/ryl) asking for a way to exclude
  lockfiles generically instead of pattern-by-pattern. ryl's file-skipping knobs (`exclude`, `per-file-ignores`,
  per-rule `ignore`) are all hand-written glob lists: no default ignore list and no lockfile awareness anywhere in the
  source (code search over `owenlamont/ryl`, 2026-11-16: only its own release tooling mentions lockfiles), and its
  docs/README demonstrate naming `pnpm-lock.yaml` by hand. The motivating example is vendir's `vendir.lock.yml` (this
  repo's vendored-skills lockfile, root `KNOWLEDGE.md` §"Vendored agent skills"): machine-regenerated on every
  `vendir sync`, never hand-edited, and emitted in a style ryl's formatter does not match, so it must be excluded from
  lint and format alike – listed in `.ryl.toml`'s `exclude` and mirrored in `hk.pkl`'s `ryl-format` step (the mirror
  exists because that step's check passes `--config-data`, which bypasses file-config discovery). Closest available
  today is a basename glob (`*.lock.yml` matches at any depth, gitignore-style) – still hand-written and over-broad,
  since it would also silence human-authored `*.lock.yml` content. Desired: something generic – built-in exclusions for
  known YAML lockfiles (`pnpm-lock.yaml`, `vendir.lock.yml`, …) or a lockfile toggle. No existing issue found searching
  `lockfile`/`exclude lock` the same day. The explicit patterns can shrink once it lands.

- Upstream: file an hk PR against [jdx/hk](https://github.com/jdx/hk) adding a `panache` builtin
  (`pkl/builtins/panache.pkl`): [panache](https://github.com/jolars/panache) is the Markdown formatter this repo runs as
  a custom hk step (`check = panache format --check {{files}}`, `fix = panache format {{files}}` over
  `**/*.md`/`**/*.markdown`), installed via the aqua registry (`aqua:jolars/panache`), so a builtin would let repos drop
  the custom step the same way the rumdl/ryl builtins do. Design point to settle in the PR: hk passes explicit file
  paths, and panache bypasses its own config excludes for explicit paths (observed here – hence the `mdExcludes` for
  `AI_POLICY.md` and `**/LICENSE.md` in `hk.pkl`); decide whether the builtin filters such files itself, documents the
  interaction, or waits for panache to honor excludes on explicit paths.

- Upstream: file an hk PR against [jdx/hk](https://github.com/jdx/hk) adding a `dockerfmt` builtin
  (`pkl/builtins/dockerfmt.pkl`): [dockerfmt](https://github.com/reteps/dockerfmt) is the Dockerfile formatter this repo
  runs as a custom hk step (`check = dockerfmt -d {{files}}`, `fix = dockerfmt -w {{files}}` over `**/Dockerfile`), so a
  builtin would let repos drop the custom step the same way the shfmt/rumdl/ryl builtins do. No hk issue or PR mentions
  dockerfmt yet (searched 2026-11-15).

- Upstream: investigate whether [shellharden](https://github.com/anordal/shellharden) mangles `for` loops and file an
  issue if none exists (check for existing ones first). Verified with v4.3.2 (2026-10): `--transform`/`--replace` quotes
  command substitutions in the iterable – `for _ in $(seq 1 120)` becomes `for _ in "$(seq 1 120)"` – which kills word
  splitting and makes the loop run exactly once (shellcheck flags the result as SC2066, error severity); an unquoted
  substitution in a for iterable is the idiomatic splitting form and not flagged by shellcheck. Minimal repro is a
  4-line script; the workaround rule (brace expansion, `read -r -a`, `mapfile`) and the 9 repo sites rewritten
  accordingly are documented in skill `ha-app-tooling`. The same run also confirmed the cosmetic nit of `[ -n "$x" ]`
  being rewritten to `[ "$x" != "" ]`. A second, worse defect (same version): the parser loses sync on nested
  parentheses inside arithmetic expansion – `printf '%04x' "$(( (a << 8) | b ))"` reports "the parser got lost" on a
  syntactically complete file, and everything after it is mangled (spurious `""` prefixes; quotes inserted into
  single-quoted strings, which corrupts generated output). Flat arithmetic (`$(( 10#$a ))`) is unaffected – but an
  arithmetic `<<` alone also breaks it (verified 2026-11, v4.3.2: `$((5 << attempt))` → "Unexpected end of file" on a
  syntactically complete file, likely lexed as a heredoc delimiter; `$((5 * 2 ** attempt))` parses and is equivalent).

# Loaded Skill: ha-app-workflow (skill)

Change and release discipline for this Home Assistant apps repository – branching, Conventional Commits, lint gates, the single-version-per-branch release rule with changelogs, CI-as-source-of-truth, device-access policy, and the version-sensitive-facts rule. Use before making any change, commit, or release in this repo.

## Content

# Change and release workflow

## Before starting

- Check the current branch first (`git status`): **Always work on a branch named `agent-<topic>`**, create one if needed
  (based off of `main`, i.e. `git switch -c agent-<topic> main`).
- If work belongs on a branch but a stray commit already landed on `main`: move it
  (`git switch -c agent-…; git branch -f main <upstream-tip>`) and disclose it to the user.
- Never stage unrelated WIP: check `git status` before staging and add files explicitly.

## Commits

- Conventional Commits (`build`, `chore:`, `ci`, `docs:`, `feat:`, `fix:`, `perf`, `refactor`, `revert`, `style`,
  `test`); scope app changes (`fix(nfs-server): …`); one commit per logical unit.
- Final trailer line: `Assisted-by: Goose:<model-slug>` – the model name without provider prefix, e.g.
  `Assisted-by: Goose:glm-5.3-flash`.
- The commit-msg hook enforces the format; escape hatch `HK=0 git commit`.

## Before finishing a change

Run `mise run check` – lint plus validate; it is the same gate CI runs. Lint-stack details and scoped checking: skill
`ha-app-tooling`. Task usage: `mise run check --help`.

## App releases

- A working branch starting from `main` bumps `version` in `config.yaml` to a **single** next version (major, minor or
  patch by semantic versioning): the branch ships one version, not one per commit, and continuously expands that
  version's `CHANGELOG.md` entry until it lands on `main`.
- Transitory extra versions within the branch are fine where testing demands one (AppArmor profile changes are only
  re-applied on app *update*, never on rebuild) – squash them back into the single version (config plus one merged
  changelog entry) before merging.
- CI enforces the rule: `.github/workflows/version-guard.yaml` fails when device-visible app files (`rootfs/`,
  `Dockerfile`, `config.yaml`, `apparmor.txt`, `translations/`) changed without a version bump – the Supervisor's update
  model makes a no-bump change a silent no-op that only repoints an already-published version tag. Exception: if the
  base version's GHCR tag was never published (its release's build/publish failed), the guard probes GHCR and passes –
  reusing the version then repoints nothing; unprovable fails closed. Changes to docs-only files (README, DOCS,
  CHANGELOG, KNOWLEDGE, TODO, `.agents/`), the per-app `.dockerignore` (it shapes the build context but never changes
  the image the device receives), and repo tooling do not require a version bump.

## CI/CD is the source of truth for what gets published

- Pushes to `main` build and publish images (`.github/workflows/builder.yaml`). If CI fails, fix the repo, not CI config
  – unless the CI config itself is wrong.
- Builder caveats: the init job needs `fetch-depth: 0` – the changed-files filter otherwise only sees the tip commit and
  silently skips multi-commit merges, so use regular merges instead of squash merges.
- The app `Dockerfile` must not pull from Docker Hub at build time (rule and rationale: skill `ha-app-scaffolding`).
- The lint workflow runs frenck's app linter natively (pinned source plus pypi requirements), not via its Docker action
  (whose Docker Hub image builds flaked with 504s and 429 runner-pool rate limits).
- In `.github/workflows/`, match GitHub users and bots by immutable user id, never by `login` (root `KNOWLEDGE.md`
  §"GitHub Actions: user identity matching").

## Device access

Testing against the real HA device over SSH only on explicit user request; otherwise hand the user exact commands to
run. On-device procedures: skill `ha-app-device-testing`.

## Version-sensitive facts

Supervisor schemas, s6-overlay layout, HAOS kernel configs and HA docs change frequently. Wherever such facts are
written down (`KNOWLEDGE.md`, comments, skills), cite the source (URL plus version/ref). Before relying on them for new
work, re-verify against the latest docs/source.

## Design change proposals

When a fix reveals a design issue, diagnose hands-on first (strace, packet captures, a reproduction lab), then explain
root cause, options and trade-offs to the user before rewriting.

## Text files

Every text file ends with a final newline (the lint gate enforces it).

# Loaded Skill: ha-app-markdown (skill)

Markdown formatting conventions for this repository – panache owns all formatting, rumdl is the semantic second linter, and specific constructs break the toolchain. Use when writing or editing any Markdown file here.

## Content

# Markdown conventions

## Formatting ownership

- panache (`panache.toml`) owns ALL formatting: `mise run fmt` reflows prose to the 120-char width. Never hand-wrap
  prose – write naturally and let `fmt` shape it.
- The lint gate runs `panache format --check` and `panache lint` over tracked `.md` files – the lint adds semantic
  checks (references, heading hierarchy, …).

## rumdl

- Second linter (`.rumdl.toml`, markdownlint-rules-rich); its own reflow is disabled (its fill state disagrees with
  panache's), so MD013 is a pure width check: code blocks exempt, lines whose only overrun is an unbreakable code span
  forgiven. panache's reflow breaks around struck spans, never inside them (it leaves a too-long span overwide on its
  own line), and MD013 does not exempt struck spans the way it exempts code spans: keep struck spans within the
  120-column width.
- Inline HTML is allow-listed per element, not per file (MD033), see `.rumdl.toml` for the currently allowed HTML tags;
  every other tag fails the lint, READMEs included. Reach for Markdown constructs (links, images, emphasis, code spans)
  before raw HTML. In tables, `table_allowed_elements` replaces (does not union with) `allowed_elements` (rumdl 0.3.1).
- rumdl never rewrites files: its fix allow-list is pinned to an inert `all` sentinel (canonicalization-preserved,

# Loaded Skill: ha-app-markdown (skill)

Markdown formatting conventions for this repository – panache owns all formatting, rumdl is the semantic second linter, and specific constructs break the toolchain. Use when writing or editing any Markdown file here.

## Content

# Markdown conventions

## Formatting ownership

- panache (`panache.toml`) owns ALL formatting: `mise run fmt` reflows prose to the 120-char width. Never hand-wrap
  prose – write naturally and let `fmt` shape it.
- The lint gate runs `panache format --check` and `panache lint` over tracked `.md` files – the lint adds semantic
  checks (references, heading hierarchy, …).

## rumdl

- Second linter (`.rumdl.toml`, markdownlint-rules-rich); its own reflow is disabled (its fill state disagrees with
  panache's), so MD013 is a pure width check: code blocks exempt, lines whose only overrun is an unbreakable code span
  forgiven. panache's reflow breaks around struck spans, never inside them (it leaves a too-long span overwide on its
  own line), and MD013 does not exempt struck spans the way it exempts code spans: keep struck spans within the
  120-column width.
- Inline HTML is allow-listed per element, not per file (MD033), see `.rumdl.toml` for the currently allowed HTML tags;
  every other tag fails the lint, READMEs included. Reach for Markdown constructs (links, images, emphasis, code spans)
  before raw HTML. In tables, `table_allowed_elements` replaces (does not union with) `allowed_elements` (rumdl 0.3.1).
- rumdl never rewrites files: its fix allow-list is pinned to an inert `all` sentinel (canonicalization-preserved,
  verified through rumdl 0.3.1; behavioral canary in `validate/apps.py`). Formatting fixes go through panache
  (`mise run fmt`); non-format rumdl findings are fixed by hand.

# Hickory DNS

## What it does

This app runs a DNS server on your Home Assistant device that answers every LAN device's DNS queries and resolves them
upstream over **encrypted DNS** (DNS-over-TLS, DNS-over-HTTPS or DNS-over-QUIC), with **DNSSEC validation** of the
answers. The point: point your router at the Home Assistant device once, and every device on the network resolves its
DNS through encrypted upstream connections – no per-device configuration, no plaintext UDP:53 queries leaving your home.

Under the hood it wraps the [`hickory-dns`](https://github.com/hickory-dns/hickory-dns) server binary in
forwarding-resolver mode: everything not answered locally is forwarded to the upstream recursive resolvers you
configure.

## Setup

   address. Every (re)connecting device then picks up the new DNS server automatically.

## CI

On every push to `main`, the [Builder](./.github/workflows/builder.yaml) workflow builds each app whose relevant files
changed and publishes its container images to GHCR via the [Build app](./.github/workflows/build-app.yaml) workflow:
per-arch images (e.g. `ghcr.io/salim-b/amd64-app-nfs-server`) plus a multi-arch manifest (e.g.
`ghcr.io/salim-b/app-nfs-server`), tagged with the app's `version` and `latest`. Each app's `image:` key in
`config.yaml` is the generic manifest name – the Builder derives the per-arch image names (`{arch}-app-<slug>`) from it
and the app's `arch:` list, so the key needs no per-arch maintenance. Pull requests only build without publishing.

(Bullet carries no citation, but the pinned voluptuous 0.16.0 is cited two bullets down for the same DSL.)

hd-idle's `main.go` (v1.22) parses `os.Args` and nothing else; the only environment variable it reads is `START_HD_IDLE`
(exits when set to `false`). `/etc/default/hd-idle` and `HD_IDLE_OPTS` are distro-packaging conventions (systemd
`EnvironmentFile=` + shell word-splitting into argv; the Alpine package does the same via its OpenRC `conf.d`). Sources:
[main.go](https://github.com/adelolmo/hd-idle/blob/v1.22/main.go),
[debian/hd-idle.service](https://github.com/adelolmo/hd-idle/blob/v1.22/debian/hd-idle.service), [v3.24
APKBUILD](https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports/-/blob/3.24-stable/community/hd-idle/APKBUILD). Alpine v3.24
ships `hd-idle 1.22-r8` (`/usr/sbin/hd-idle`, no runtime deps; v1.22 is a GitHub tag without a release; pkgrel bumps so
far are toolchain rebuilds with an unchanged CLI).

`diskstats/snapshot.go` (v1.22) matches `/proc/diskstats` names against `sd[a-z]+$` (disk) and `dm-*$` (dm → holder
disk); anything else (`nvme*`, `mmcblk*`, `loop*`, `ram*`) is never touched – system disks on SD/eMMC/NVMe are out of
hd-idle's reach (third exclusion layer), and NVMe drives cannot be managed at all. The upstream PARTITION matching
(`sd[a-z]+[0-9]+$`) is commented out in v1.22 – partitions are invisible to the daemon; per-partition activity still
wakes the configured disk only because the kernel accumulates partition I/O into the disk's own counters. dm attribution
picks a single holder – upstream reads `/sys/class/block/<dm>/holders/` via `os.ReadDir` (lexicographic order,
deterministic; the app's own attribution is likewise single-holder): a multi-holder dm device (multi-PV LVM) cannot be
managed correctly; the common dm-crypt case (one holder) is exact. Source:
[snapshot.go](https://github.com/adelolmo/hd-idle/blob/v1.22/diskstats/snapshot.go).


Two independent AppArmor gates, both must be open: (1) the SG_IO ioctl is mediated only via the file's r/w permission
(no per-command mediation until AppArmor 4; mechanism: repository-root `KNOWLEDGE.md` §"AppArmor: mediation and profile
mechanics") – `/dev/sd* rwk,` plus the `file,` blanket covers it; (2) the kernel's `capable(CAP_SYS_RAWIO)` check inside
`scsi_cmd_allowed()` is mediated by AppArmor itself (same root section) – both profiles need `capability sys_rawio,`.
Without (2) every ata-path command failed with EPERM despite the container capability: capable() returned false and
`scsi_cmd_allowed()` fell through to `return open_for_write` (the EPERM source for O_RDONLY fds).

**Why the capability cannot be tightened**: AppArmor capability rules enumerate whole capabilities (they mediate the
kernel's boolean `capable()` check – apparmor.d(5)), so a fraction of `CAP_SYS_RAWIO` is not expressible; per-command
ioctl mediation does not exist upstream; HAOS ships AppArmor 3.1.7. **Both grant sites are needed**: the daemon
sub-profile (ata spindowns) and the top profile (pmfix's smartctl ATA SET FEATURES is the same non-read-safe class;
`hd-idle -t` runs in the top profile, e.g. the lab's `docker exec`). What the capability additionally unlocks in this
container (capabilities(7)): `/proc/kcore` reads (kernel-gated on capable(CAP_SYS_RAWIO), file side allowed by the
`file,` blanket – genuinely reachable for a compromised process; the accepted residual risk of the ata path) and
`ioperm`/`iopl` (x86/amd64). Closed surfaces: `/dev/mem`, `/dev/kmem`, `/dev/port`, `/dev/cpu/*/msr` (outside the
supervisor's device-cgroup allowlist); `mmap_min_addr` (moot: `/proc/sys` mounted read-only); SCSI commands to other
nodes (device cgroup); seccomp could trim further but the supervisor exposes no per-app seccomp customization.

        _LOGGER.info("Phase '%s' starting %d apps", stage, len(tasks))

#!/usr/bin/with-contenv bashio
# shellcheck shell=bash
set -euo pipefail

## Validate the app configuration and generate the hd-idle command line (/etc/hd-idle.args, consumed by the s6-rc
## hd-idle service). The logic lives in the shared hd-idle-genargs helper so the hd-idle-watch longrun can re-run it.

bashio::log.info "Configuring hd-idle..."
if /usr/bin/hd-idle-genargs /etc/hd-idle.args; then
  ## Drive-PM treatment at boot (re-applied by the watcher on drive (re)appearance); runs unconditionally (the
  ## drives file's pm-flag column carries the effective per-drive decision), non-fatal – the treatment is best-effort.
  /usr/bin/hd-idle-pmfix /etc/hd-idle.drives \
    || bashio::log.warning "hd-idle-pmfix failed - the drives' power management stays as is."
  exit 0
fi
exit 1

Acquired: 2026-11-16
Snippets:
A top-level `exclude` lists paths ryl skips entirely. No rule runs against them, `ryl format` leaves them alone, and they produce no diagnostics. `--exclude <GLOBS>` replaces config exclusions, including patterns loaded through `exclude-from-file`, for one run. Pass comma-separated gitignore-style globs once per command, anchored at the current working directory rather than the config: ``` ryl check --enable ALL --exclude 'pnpm-lock.yaml,vendor/**' . ryl format --exclude 'generated/**' . ``` `--exclude ''` clears the config's exclusions. Explicit file arguments remain subject to exclusions. Git ignore handling during directory walks is unchanged.

Title: ryl/docs/getting-started/migrating-from-yamllint.md at main · owenlamont/ryl
URL: https://github.com/owenlamont/ryl/blob/main/docs/getting-started/migrating-from-yamllint.md
Acquired: 2026-10-18
Snippets:
``` ryl check --enable ALL --disable line-length,truthy,document-start --exclude pnpm-lock.yaml . ``` `ALL` selects every ryl rule, rather than yamllint's `default` preset. `--disable` subtracts from config or `--enable` selections; `--exclude` replaces config exclusions with comma-separated globs relative to the current directory. Both flags may appear once. TOML still has no `extends` or presets.
[...]
Migration produces a self-contained config. yamllint's top-level `ignore` and `ignore-from-file` become `exclude` and `exclude-from-file`, since in ryl TOML per-rule `ignore` suppresses one rule; top-level `ignore` remains a deprecated alias for whole-file `exclude`. A relative `extends` is flattened (its rules are inlined), resolved relative to the config's own directory first, then the current directory. A user-global config with a relative `ignore-from-file`, at either the top level or rule level, is skipped with a warning: the path resolves against each linted file's directory, which a single migrated config cannot express. Make the path absolute or move the setting into a project config, then re-run. Absolute top-level paths are inlined as `exclude` patterns; absolute rule-level paths are retained. Project migration keeps a relative `ignore-from-file` as-is, because the `.ryl.toml` stays in the same directory.

A user-global config with a relative `ignore-from-file`, at either the top level or rule level, is skipped with a warning: the path resolves against each linted file's directory, which a single migrated config cannot express. Make the path absolute or move the setting into a project config, then re-run. Absolute top-level paths are inlined as `exclude` patterns; absolute rule-level paths are retained. Project migration keeps a relative `ignore-from-file` as-is, because the `.ryl.toml` stays in the same directory.

## Supervisor: option schema quirks

- `match(...)` regexes in `config.yaml` schema fields use voluptuous `Match` (*search* semantics, not fullmatch) –
  always anchor with explicit `^…$`.
- The supervisor's schema-element parser breaks on literal `\t`/`\n` inside YAML double-quoted scalars (they become real
  control characters) – express whitespace classes as `\\s` instead.

## Deploy tasks: local builds and store-copy conflicts

With a top-level `image:` key set, the supervisor **pulls that image from GHCR** instead of building the app folder
locally – an image-based app never rebuilds from source (see the [dev docs on remote
development](https://contributors.home-assistant.io/apps/guides/testing/#remote-development)). The repo's device deploy
tasks (`deploy:local`, and `test:live` through it) therefore comment the key out in the *device-side* copy of the app's
`config.yaml`.

Two installations of the same app cannot coexist on one device – they conflict on the app's published ports. A
supervisor reject the update with `method 'manual' requires at least an address`), then `ha dns restart`.

The same mirroring also blocks on-device image builds (`deploy:local`) on devices whose only working plaintext resolver
is the device itself: the buildkit CLI container resolves the registry through a copy of the host's `resolv.conf`, and a
host-networked resolver answers container-sourced UDP queries with the egress route's gateway address as source IP
(per-route source selection), which DNS clients discard as source-mismatched – the build fails at
`load metadata for <base image>` before any `RUN` step runs. Substituting `172.30.32.3` as the host resolver triggers
the loop death above instead. Such devices can only take registry-deployed images (`deploy:registry`).

  `options=(bind)` instead. Mount sources are matched as passed: busybox passes the device string for pseudo-filesystems

## apk package version policy

**Official apps' practice** (home-assistant/addons, verified 2026-10): apk packages **float** (`dnsmasq`, `samba`,
`mariadb`, `vlc`: bare `apk add --no-cache <pkg>`), while version-sensitive *cores* are pinned explicitly via
`build.yaml` ARGs (mosquitto, letsencrypt's certbot/cryptography stack, whisper's pip stack). Floating apk packages
means released images get newer package content on rebuilds without a version bump; existing installs keep the old
digest until the next versioned release.

**Our policy** splits by coupling:
carries every drifted pin and stays self-consistent (all updates sharing a `groupName` go into one branch/PR; Renovate
docs, configuration-options: groupName/rebaseWhen, verified 2026-11-12). Residual edge: independent packages pinned in
one Dockerfile can drift with different update types – the two group branches then both touch that Dockerfile and the
automerging pkgrel PR stays red until the pkgver PR merges (its build needs the newer sibling pin); the pkgrel group
then rebases when behind base (rebaseWhen auto: behind-base-branch for automerging branches) and automerges, so the
delay is bounded by the pkgver review. The version-guard workflow still passes on the Renovate PR as opened.
`postUpgradeTasks` need `allowedPostUpgradeCommands` – a self-hosted-only option – so the changelog entry is filled
post-merge by the CI changelog job instead. The rule's registryUrls branch value must be updated together with the

## HA base image: shell gotchas

Facts; the safe procedures (procfs writes, suppression of failed-redirection diagnostics, environment passing, PATH,
bashio stubbing): skill `ha-app-base-image`.

- **`echo`/`printf` emit a single `writev(2)`**: the base image's bash (5.3.9) implements the output of its `echo` and
  `printf` builtins as one `writev(2)` call, with the text and the trailing newline as separate iovecs. Kernel files
  that only implement the old-style single-buffer `.write` and no `.write_iter` (many procfs/sysfs transaction files,
  e.g. `/proc/fs/nfsd/*`) reject `writev(2)` with `EINVAL` – producing a misleading `write error: Invalid argument` that
  is about the syscall *shape*, not the written content. Callers that do a single `write(2)` (busybox `echo`, `cat`,
  many C daemons' own writes) succeed. (Which files this bites in a given app: the app's `KNOWLEDGE.md`.)
- **Failed redirections bypass the command's `2>/dev/null`**: a failed redirection is diagnosed by the shell itself,
  *before* the command's own redirections are in effect.
- **`with-contenv` wipes the inherited environment unless `S6_KEEP_ENV=1`**: the s6-overlay shebang helper runs
  `emptyenv -p` and then imports only `/run/s6/container_environment` (the variables the supervisor/s6 boot provides).

## apk package version policy

**Official apps' practice** (home-assistant/addons, verified 2026-10): apk packages **float** (`dnsmasq`, `samba`,
`mariadb`, `vlc`: bare `apk add --no-cache <pkg>`), while version-sensitive *cores* are pinned explicitly via
`build.yaml` ARGs (mosquitto, letsencrypt's certbot/cryptography stack, whisper's pip stack). Floating apk packages
means released images get newer package content on rebuilds without a version bump; existing installs keep the old
digest until the next versioned release.

**Our policy** splits by coupling:
carries every drifted pin and stays self-consistent (all updates sharing a `groupName` go into one branch/PR; Renovate
docs, configuration-options: groupName/rebaseWhen, verified 2026-11-12). Residual edge: independent packages pinned in
one Dockerfile can drift with different update types – the two group branches then both touch that Dockerfile and the
automerging pkgrel PR stays red until the pkgver PR merges (its build needs the newer sibling pin); the pkgrel group
then rebases when behind base (rebaseWhen auto: behind-base-branch for automerging branches) and automerges, so the
delay is bounded by the pkgver review. The version-guard workflow still passes on the Renovate PR as opened.
`postUpgradeTasks` need `allowedPostUpgradeCommands` – a self-hosted-only option – so the changelog entry is filled
post-merge by the CI changelog job instead. The rule's registryUrls branch value must be updated together with the
Dockerfile's `BUILD_FROM` default on a base-image bump; the validate:apk-pins task derives the branch dynamically and
## HA base image: shell gotchas

Facts; the safe procedures (procfs writes, suppression of failed-redirection diagnostics, environment passing, PATH,
bashio stubbing): skill `ha-app-base-image`.

- **`echo`/`printf` emit a single `writev(2)`**: the base image's bash (5.3.9) implements the output of its `echo` and
  `printf` builtins as one `writev(2)` call, with the text and the trailing newline as separate iovecs. Kernel files
  that only implement the old-style single-buffer `.write` and no `.write_iter` (many procfs/sysfs transaction files,
  e.g. `/proc/fs/nfsd/*`) reject `writev(2)` with `EINVAL` – producing a misleading `write error: Invalid argument` that
  is about the syscall *shape*, not the written content. Callers that do a single `write(2)` (busybox `echo`, `cat`,
  many C daemons' own writes) succeed. (Which files this bites in a given app: the app's `KNOWLEDGE.md`.)
- **Failed redirections bypass the command's `2>/dev/null`**: a failed redirection is diagnosed by the shell itself,
  *before* the command's own redirections are in effect.
- **`with-contenv` wipes the inherited environment unless `S6_KEEP_ENV=1`**: the s6-overlay shebang helper runs
  `emptyenv -p` and then imports only `/run/s6/container_environment` (the variables the supervisor/s6 boot provides).

## Supervisor: DNS resolution chain (CoreDNS)

The HAOS host and containers resolve through the CoreDNS plugin, whose forward priority is: manual `servers` (the DNS
options), then `locals` (the host's NetworkManager/DHCP-learned DNS servers, exposed as `dns://<ip>` entries), then
CloudFlare DoT when `fallback` is true (`supervisor/plugins/dns.py::_write_config`, ref `6556811`, checked 2026-11-02).
`GET /dns/info` returns `data.servers`, `data.locals` and `data.fallback`; the device's own LAN IPs come from
`GET /network/info` (`data.interfaces[].ipv4.address` / `.ipv6.address`, CIDR-suffixed strings, v1 shape; the v2 shape
nests them under `state`/`config` instead). If the device's DNS servers include the device's own IP, the device resolves
through whatever app serves :53 on it – uninstalling that app (e.g. a locally installed hickory-dns) cuts the
supervisor's own DNS off mid-task, so subsequent registry downloads fail.

Setting a host DNS server equal to the CoreDNS plugin's own address (`GET /dns/info` `data.host`, `172.30.32.3` on
standard installs) is fatal: CoreDNS's loop probe detects the self-loop and the container exits (CoreDNS log
`plugin/loop: Loop` → exit 1). The supervisor raises the `dns_loop` issue and rewrites the config dropping both
`servers` and `locals` (fallback-DoT-only config, `supervisor/plugins/dns.py::_write_config`, ref `6556811`), but the
watchdog does not reliably revive the dead container – observed on-device 2026-11-12, where it stayed dead across two
network reconfigurations until `ha dns restart`. Since `locals` always mirrors the host's NetworkManager nameservers,
the CoreDNS plugin can therefore never be the host's own resolver. Recovery order after such an outage: restore the host
DNS servers (`ha network update <iface> --ipv4-method auto --ipv4-nameserver <ip>…`; omitting `--ipv4-method` makes the
supervisor reject the update with `method 'manual' requires at least an address`), then `ha dns restart`.

The same mirroring also blocks on-device image builds (`deploy:local`) on devices whose only working plaintext resolver
is the device itself: the buildkit CLI container resolves the registry through a copy of the host's `resolv.conf`, and a
host-networked resolver answers container-sourced UDP queries with the egress route's gateway address as source IP
(per-route source selection), which DNS clients discard as source-mismatched – the build fails at
`load metadata for <base image>` before any `RUN` step runs. Substituting `172.30.32.3` as the host resolver triggers
the loop death above instead. Such devices can only take registry-deployed images (`deploy:registry`).

Runtime semantics of the generated `/etc/exports` content (schema-side constraints are repository-wide: root
`KNOWLEDGE.md` §"Supervisor: option schema quirks"):

- The kernel keeps a single export cache entry per (path, client); duplicate lines resolve by *last line wins* –
  identical duplicates are noise, conflicting options silently apply whichever line is last (order-dependent). Hence
  duplicate (path, network) share entries are rejected: one option set applies per pair (the same path with different
  networks is legitimate).
- The per-share `fsid=` is assigned by config order (a counter): editing the share list renumbers the followers – NFSv4
  filehandles embed the fsid, so a renumber makes clients' old handles stale, including their recovery records after a
  share edit + app restart. An existing wart that only matters across share-list edits.
  filesystem's UUID, and filehandles keyed by that UUID are ambiguous once multiple exports share one filesystem (binds
  of the same fs) – they resolve back to the wrong export (mounts land on the read-only pseudo root → `EROFS` on write).
- The pseudo root needs no `crossmnt` (an NFSv3-era flag for seeing mounts beneath an export point): NFSv4 clients
  switch the export at mountpoint crossings regardless (`nfsd_cross_mnt` consults the export cache for any v4 client),
  and the pseudo entries mountd synthesizes carry `crossmnt` anyway.

## Grace period

Every restart cycle of the kernel server (`rpc.nfsd 0` + start) starts a grace period (default 90 s) during which
clients' write opens get `NFS4ERR_GRACE` and retry – writes appear to stall; a client-side write attempt in the window
fails with `EINTR` (busybox ash: `can't create …: Interrupted system call`). With the shipped `nfsdcld` tracker the
grace is only paid when client records exist: fresh boots skip it via the kernel's fast path (needs
`track_reclaim_completes`, set by the cld-v2 tracker init – `nfs4_state_start_net`'s skip path), and the grace ends
early once all recorded clients have reclaimed. The app's `--grace-time` default matches the lease time. Writes to
`/proc/fs/nfsd/v4_end_grace` end the grace regardless of any tracker (v6.18: the only guard is a running server, else
`EBUSY`) – but that would deny late reclaimers their window, so it is not a useful lever for a server that wants clients
to recover.

  nfsdcld 2.6.x answers GetVersion with upcall protocol version 2.
- Across a server recreation (connected client, held exclusive flock): the reloaded record makes the kernel run a grace
  period instead of skipping it, the client reclaims, the flock survives, the grace ends early once the reclaiming
  client is back; the store lives on `/data`, untouched by watcher cycles or app restarts.
- Residual unknown, NFSv4.0 early grace: the "all clients done reclaiming" printk only fires via RECLAIM_COMPLETE (the
  Linux client sends it only for v4.1, `fs/nfs/nfs4proc.c` `nfs40_reboot_recovery_ops`), and the laundromat cannot fire
  before the configured grace on its own – yet the observed grace end always followed the reclaim promptly; most
  plausible: reclaim events plus immediate laundromat kicks ending the grace once nobody is still reclaiming
  (`clients_still_reclaiming`). Only re-verify if this ever looks wrong.
- App wiring: cont-init mounts rpc_pipefs non-fatally (failure = degraded mode, the old short-grace behavior) and
  creates `/data/nfsdcld`; the `nfsd` oneshot depends on the `cld` longrun. AppArmor grants: §"AppArmor profile –

Runtime semantics of the generated `/etc/exports` content (schema-side constraints are repository-wide: root
`KNOWLEDGE.md` §"Supervisor: option schema quirks"):

- The kernel keeps a single export cache entry per (path, client); duplicate lines resolve by *last line wins* –
  identical duplicates are noise, conflicting options silently apply whichever line is last (order-dependent). Hence
  duplicate (path, network) share entries are rejected: one option set applies per pair (the same path with different
  networks is legitimate).
- The per-share `fsid=` is assigned by config order (a counter): editing the share list renumbers the followers – NFSv4
  filehandles embed the fsid, so a renumber makes clients' old handles stale, including their recovery records after a
  share edit + app restart. An existing wart that only matters across share-list edits.
  filesystem's UUID, and filehandles keyed by that UUID are ambiguous once multiple exports share one filesystem (binds
  of the same fs) – they resolve back to the wrong export (mounts land on the read-only pseudo root → `EROFS` on write).
- The pseudo root needs no `crossmnt` (an NFSv3-era flag for seeing mounts beneath an export point): NFSv4 clients
  switch the export at mountpoint crossings regardless (`nfsd_cross_mnt` consults the export cache for any v4 client),
  and the pseudo entries mountd synthesizes carry `crossmnt` anyway.

## Grace period

Every restart cycle of the kernel server (`rpc.nfsd 0` + start) starts a grace period (default 90 s) during which
clients' write opens get `NFS4ERR_GRACE` and retry – writes appear to stall; a client-side write attempt in the window
fails with `EINTR` (busybox ash: `can't create …: Interrupted system call`). With the shipped `nfsdcld` tracker the
grace is only paid when client records exist: fresh boots skip it via the kernel's fast path (needs
`track_reclaim_completes`, set by the cld-v2 tracker init – `nfs4_state_start_net`'s skip path), and the grace ends
early once all recorded clients have reclaimed. The app's `--grace-time` default matches the lease time. Writes to
`/proc/fs/nfsd/v4_end_grace` end the grace regardless of any tracker (v6.18: the only guard is a running server, else
`EBUSY`) – but that would deny late reclaimers their window, so it is not a useful lever for a server that wants clients
to recover.

  nfsdcld 2.6.x answers GetVersion with upcall protocol version 2.
- Across a server recreation (connected client, held exclusive flock): the reloaded record makes the kernel run a grace
  period instead of skipping it, the client reclaims, the flock survives, the grace ends early once the reclaiming
  client is back; the store lives on `/data`, untouched by watcher cycles or app restarts.
- Residual unknown, NFSv4.0 early grace: the "all clients done reclaiming" printk only fires via RECLAIM_COMPLETE (the
  Linux client sends it only for v4.1, `fs/nfs/nfs4proc.c` `nfs40_reboot_recovery_ops`), and the laundromat cannot fire
  before the configured grace on its own – yet the observed grace end always followed the reclaim promptly; most
  plausible: reclaim events plus immediate laundromat kicks ending the grace once nobody is still reclaiming
  (`clients_still_reclaiming`). Only re-verify if this ever looks wrong.
- App wiring: cont-init mounts rpc_pipefs non-fatally (failure = degraded mode, the old short-grace behavior) and
  creates `/data/nfsdcld`; the `nfsd` oneshot depends on the `cld` longrun. AppArmor grants: §"AppArmor profile –

## Content

# Markdown conventions

## Formatting ownership

- panache (`panache.toml`) owns ALL formatting: `mise run fmt` reflows prose to the 120-char width. Never hand-wrap
  prose – write naturally and let `fmt` shape it.
- The lint gate runs `panache format --check` and `panache lint` over tracked `.md` files – the lint adds semantic
  checks (references, heading hierarchy, …).

## rumdl

- Second linter (`.rumdl.toml`, markdownlint-rules-rich); its own reflow is disabled (its fill state disagrees with
  panache's), so MD013 is a pure width check: code blocks exempt, lines whose only overrun is an unbreakable code span
  forgiven. panache's reflow breaks around struck spans, never inside them (it leaves a too-long span overwide on its
  own line), and MD013 does not exempt struck spans the way it exempts code spans: keep struck spans within the
  120-column width.
- Inline HTML is allow-listed per element, not per file (MD033), see `.rumdl.toml` for the currently allowed HTML tags;
  every other tag fails the lint, READMEs included. Reach for Markdown constructs (links, images, emphasis, code spans)
  before raw HTML. In tables, `table_allowed_elements` replaces (does not union with) `allowed_elements` (rumdl 0.3.1).
- rumdl never rewrites files: its fix allow-list is pinned to an inert `all` sentinel (canonicalization-preserved,
  verified through rumdl 0.3.1; behavioral canary in `validate/apps.py`). Formatting fixes go through panache
  (`mise run fmt`); non-format rumdl findings are fixed by hand.

# Loaded Skill: ha-app-workflow (skill)

Change and release discipline for this Home Assistant apps repository – branching, Conventional Commits, lint gates, the single-version-per-branch release rule with changelogs, CI-as-source-of-truth, device-access policy, and the version-sensitive-facts rule. Use before making any change, commit, or release in this repo.

## Content

# Change and release workflow

## Before starting

- Check the current branch first (`git status`): **Always work on a branch named `agent-<topic>`**, create one if needed
  (based off of `main`, i.e. `git switch -c agent-<topic> main`).
- If work belongs on a branch but a stray commit already landed on `main`: move it
  (`git switch -c agent-…; git branch -f main <upstream-tip>`) and disclose it to the user.
- Never stage unrelated WIP: check `git status` before staging and add files explicitly.

## Commits

- Conventional Commits (`build`, `chore:`, `ci`, `docs:`, `feat:`, `fix:`, `perf`, `refactor`, `revert`, `style`,
  `test`); scope app changes (`fix(nfs-server): …`); one commit per logical unit.
- Final trailer line: `Assisted-by: Goose:<model-slug>` – the model name without provider prefix, e.g.
  `Assisted-by: Goose:glm-5.3-flash`.
- The commit-msg hook enforces the format; escape hatch `HK=0 git commit`.

## Before finishing a change

Run `mise run check` – lint plus validate; it is the same gate CI runs. Lint-stack details and scoped checking: skill
`ha-app-tooling`. Task usage: `mise run check --help`.

## App releases

- A working branch starting from `main` bumps `version` in `config.yaml` to a **single** next version (major, minor or
  patch by semantic versioning): the branch ships one version, not one per commit, and continuously expands that
  version's `CHANGELOG.md` entry until it lands on `main`.
- Transitory extra versions within the branch are fine where testing demands one (AppArmor profile changes are only
  re-applied on app *update*, never on rebuild) – squash them back into the single version (config plus one merged
  changelog entry) before merging.
- CI enforces the rule: `.github/workflows/version-guard.yaml` fails when device-visible app files (`rootfs/`,
  `Dockerfile`, `config.yaml`, `apparmor.txt`, `translations/`) changed without a version bump – the Supervisor's update
  model makes a no-bump change a silent no-op that only repoints an already-published version tag. Exception: if the
  base version's GHCR tag was never published (its release's build/publish failed), the guard probes GHCR and passes –
  reusing the version then repoints nothing; unprovable fails closed. Changes to docs-only files (README, DOCS,
  CHANGELOG, KNOWLEDGE, TODO, `.agents/`), the per-app `.dockerignore` (it shapes the build context but never changes
  the image the device receives), and repo tooling do not require a version bump.

## CI/CD is the source of truth for what gets published

- Pushes to `main` build and publish images (`.github/workflows/builder.yaml`). If CI fails, fix the repo, not CI config
  – unless the CI config itself is wrong.
- Builder caveats: the init job needs `fetch-depth: 0` – the changed-files filter otherwise only sees the tip commit and
  silently skips multi-commit merges, so use regular merges instead of squash merges.
- The app `Dockerfile` must not pull from Docker Hub at build time (rule and rationale: skill `ha-app-scaffolding`).
- The lint workflow runs frenck's app linter natively (pinned source plus pypi requirements), not via its Docker action
  (whose Docker Hub image builds flaked with 504s and 429 runner-pool rate limits).
- In `.github/workflows/`, match GitHub users and bots by immutable user id, never by `login` (root `KNOWLEDGE.md`
  §"GitHub Actions: user identity matching").

## Device access

Testing against the real HA device over SSH only on explicit user request; otherwise hand the user exact commands to
run. On-device procedures: skill `ha-app-device-testing`.

## Version-sensitive facts

Supervisor schemas, s6-overlay layout, HAOS kernel configs and HA docs change frequently. Wherever such facts are
written down (`KNOWLEDGE.md`, comments, skills), cite the source (URL plus version/ref). Before relying on them for new
work, re-verify against the latest docs/source.

## Design change proposals

When a fix reveals a design issue, diagnose hands-on first (strace, packet captures, a reproduction lab), then explain
root cause, options and trade-offs to the user before rewriting.

## Text files

Every text file ends with a final newline (the lint gate enforces it).

Authoring rules (authoritative, from this repo's AGENTS.md):

PLACEMENT – never duplicate information across files; each piece has exactly one canonical home:
- README.md (root): human users (what the repo is, install) + human developers (§"Development" getting-started).
- Root KNOWLEDGE.md: cross-app technical facts (supervisor behaviors, AppArmor mechanics, base-image shell gotchas, apk policy). <app>/KNOWLEDGE.md: app-specific cross-session facts.
- .agents/skills/<name>/: procedures for coding agents; skills cite facts from knowledge files by exact § name, never restate them.
- <app>/DOCS.md: end-user documentation; must not duplicate option field descriptions from <app>/translations/en.yaml – point at the UI instead.
- <app>/CHANGELOG.md: user-visible changes per version. TODO.md (root + per-app): open work items only; resolved items deleted, not archived (git history is the record).
- AGENTS.md: agent process and placement rule only – no facts, no procedures.
- Code/config comments: minimum; purpose plus pointer (e.g. "See <app>/KNOWLEDGE.md §…"); must not restate facts recorded elsewhere.

PARSIMONY – no episodic content in current-state prose: no references to past states, working history ("this used to…", "we switched from X to Y"), or things of little future relevance. Comments are exceptions, not defaults. EXEMPT from "episodic" flagging: (1) CHANGELOG entries – they ARE the history; (2) version-sensitive-fact citations (URL + version/ref + checked-date) – required by the workflow rule; (3) TODO status notes. But flag: commit-SHA references used as prose provenance for a past state (vs fact-anchoring citations which are fine), duplicated facts within one file, prose restating what a cited section already says.

TYPOGRAPHY – dash punctuation is the spaced en dash " – ", never a bare spaced hyphen " - " or an em dash "—"; numeric ranges take an unspaced en dash (3–5); compound modifiers (drive-PM), code, keys, flags keep the plain hyphen. Applies only to files in your scope, NOT to vendored files (.agents/skills/entire-*, .entire/).

Version-sensitive facts (supervisor schemas, CLI, kernels, HAOS) in root KNOWLEDGE.md were fully re-verified against primary sources on 2026-11-23 (yesterday). Do NOT attempt external re-verification and do NOT flag date-stamped citations as stale merely for being a day old. This audit is about internal consistency + rule conformance only.

We support using AI (i.e., LLMs) as tools when contributing to Open Home Foundation projects. However, you are responsible for any contributions you submit, and we are responsible for any contributions we merge and release. We hold a high bar for all contributions to our projects.

**We do not allow autonomous agents to be used for contributing to our projects.** We will close any pull requests or issues that we believe were created autonomously, and may mark automated comments as spam. This includes contributions that bypass the provided issue or pull request templates.

We don't mind if you use AI tools to help you write. However, do not have tools post unreviewed content on your behalf. Keep responses to the minimum needed to communicate your intent. We may hide any comments that we believe are unreviewed AI output.

# Changelog

## 0.3.5

- Internals: no behavior change – the `Dockerfile` is reformatted to the repository's uniform `dockerfmt` style
  (continuation-line indentation; the built image is unchanged). No configuration change.

## 0.3.4

- Internals: no behavior change – `config.yaml` is reformatted to the repository's uniform `ryl format` style (quote
  normalization; the parsed configuration is unchanged). No configuration change.

## 0.3.3

- Internals: no behavior change – the profile's blanket `signal,` rule is gone. Every signal path the app has is already
  granted by `<abstractions/base>` (AppArmor 3.1.7): same-label delivery (s6-supervise signals the daemon on stop, shell
  job control), signal-existence probes, and receive from the unconfined host runtime (how `docker stop`/restart reach
  PID 1). The blanket's extra grants – cross-label send/receive against arbitrary labels – are unexercisable here: the

## Limitations

- **Only `sd*` disks are monitored**: NVMe, SD/eMMC and loop devices are never touched (details in the
  [documentation](/config/app/f8b2d53d_hd-idle/documentation)).
- **Do not run other disk-monitoring tools alongside**: SMART polling keeps waking the drives.
- **Spin-up wear**: Shorter idle times result in more drive spin-ups, which eventually wear out the spindle motor and
  bearings; keep it at 3–5 minutes minimum (hd-idle's default is 10 minutes).

## Documentation

For usage, configuration and security notes, see the [**Documentation**](/config/app/f8b2d53d_hd-idle/documentation).

=== hd-idle README 25-35 ===
## Limitations

- **Only `sd*` disks are monitored**: NVMe, SD/eMMC and loop devices are never touched (details in the
  [documentation](/config/app/f8b2d53d_hd-idle/documentation)).
- **Do not run other disk-monitoring tools alongside**: SMART polling keeps waking the drives.
- **Spin-up wear**: Shorter idle times result in more drive spin-ups, which eventually wear out the spindle motor and
  bearings; keep it at 3–5 minutes minimum (hd-idle's default is 10 minutes).

## Documentation

For usage, configuration and security notes, see the [**Documentation**](/config/app/f8b2d53d_hd-idle/documentation).

          # only ever touches `uses:` pin lines – precisely the change the
          # review assesses. Normalizing a digest that is followed only by
          # whitespace (the version comment) or end of line therefore passes
          # digest+comment rewrites of any pin, while any other change to the
          # file – new steps, changed arguments, a dropped guard – is
          # tampering. A digest repointed to a longer ref (hex extension or
          # non-hex suffix) or to a floating ref fails to normalize and
          # trips, failing closed.
          sanitize() {
            # A revision predating this file (dispatch on an older PR) yields
            # empty output on both sides and passes the comparison.
            git show "$1:.github/workflows/action-bump-review.yaml" 2>/dev/null |
              sed -E 's/(uses:[[:space:]]*[^@[:space:]]+)@[0-9a-f]{40}([[:space:]].*)?$/\1@DIGEST/'

## Supervisor: store slugs (in-app documentation links)

- Installing an app **from an app repository** gives it the installed slug `<hash>_<slug>` where hash = the first 8 hex
  of `sha1(lowercased_repository_url)` (`supervisor/store/utils.py` `get_hash_from_repository`; verified numerically
  2026-10: `sha1("https://github.com/salim-b/home-assistant-apps-salim")[:8]` = `f8b2d53d`). Local test installs under
  `/local_apps/` get `local_<slug>`.
- In-app links (`README.md`/`DOCS.md` `/config/app/<hash>_<slug>/...`) must use the hashed form to work for the
  repository install (the normal user case); they are dead links for local test installs – expected, those are dev-only.

## Supervisor: DNS resolution chain (CoreDNS)

The HAOS host and containers resolve through the CoreDNS plugin, whose forward priority is: manual `servers` (the DNS
options), then `locals` (the host's NetworkManager/DHCP-learned DNS servers, exposed as `dns://<ip>` entries), then
CloudFlare DoT when `fallback` is true (`supervisor/plugins/dns.py::_write_config`, ref `6556811`, checked 2026-11-02).
`GET /dns/info` returns `data.servers`, `data.locals` and `data.fallback`; the device's own LAN IPs come from
`GET /network/info` (`data.interfaces[].ipv4.address` / `.ipv6.address`, CIDR-suffixed strings, v1 shape; the v2 shape
nests them under `state`/`config` instead). If the device's DNS servers include the device's own IP, the device resolves
through whatever app serves :53 on it – uninstalling that app (e.g. a locally installed hickory-dns) cuts the
supervisor's own DNS off mid-task, so subsequent registry downloads fail.

Setting a host DNS server equal to the CoreDNS plugin's own address (`GET /dns/info` `data.host`, `172.30.32.3` on
standard installs) is fatal: CoreDNS's loop probe detects the self-loop and the container exits (CoreDNS log
`plugin/loop: Loop` → exit 1). The supervisor raises the `dns_loop` issue and rewrites the config dropping both
`servers` and `locals` (fallback-DoT-only config, `supervisor/plugins/dns.py::_write_config`, ref `6556811`), but the
watchdog does not reliably revive the dead container – observed on-device 2026-11-12, where it stayed dead across two
network reconfigurations until `ha dns restart`. Since `locals` always mirrors the host's NetworkManager nameservers,
the CoreDNS plugin can therefore never be the host's own resolver. Recovery order after such an outage: restore the host
DNS servers (`ha network update <iface> --ipv4-method auto --ipv4-nameserver <ip>…`; omitting `--ipv4-method` defaults
the update to static method `manual`, which NetworkManager rejects for an address-less profile), then `ha dns restart`.

The same mirroring also blocks on-device image builds (`deploy:local`) on devices whose only working plaintext resolver
is the device itself: the buildkit CLI container resolves the registry through a copy of the host's `resolv.conf`, and a
host-networked resolver answers container-sourced UDP queries with the egress route's gateway address as source IP
(per-route source selection), which DNS clients discard as source-mismatched – the build fails at
`load metadata for <base image>` before any `RUN` step runs. Substituting `172.30.32.3` as the host resolver triggers
the loop death above instead. Such devices can only take registry-deployed images (`deploy:registry`).

3. hd-idle itself only ever monitors `sd*` disks; system disks on SD/eMMC/NVMe are out of its reach anyway.

### Hotplug behavior

Drives are granted device access dynamically by the supervisor – including when re-attached later, without an app
restart. A drive that is detached when the app starts is passed to hd-idle for runtime resolution (by-id symlinks are
re-resolved once the drive appears) – and hd-idle applies its configured idle time to it immediately upon resolution,
without waiting for a configuration restart. The app also periodically re-resolves its configured drives: after moving
drives between ports or machines – which changes their kernel names (`/dev/sda`, `/dev/sdb`, ...) – hd-idle is restarted
automatically with the updated configuration (within about half a minute); no manual restart is needed.

## Activity log and debugging

Spin-down/spin-up events always appear in the app log. **Debug mode** adds a per-monitoring-cycle state dump for every
disk (useful when drives refuse to spin down); **Activity log** writes per-drive run/standby records to
`/data/hd-idle.log` – both field descriptions in the options UI have the details.

## Supervisor: DNS resolution chain (CoreDNS)

The HAOS host and containers resolve through the CoreDNS plugin, whose forward priority is: manual `servers` (the DNS
options), then `locals` (the host's NetworkManager/DHCP-learned DNS servers, exposed as `dns://<ip>` entries), then
CloudFlare DoT when `fallback` is true (`supervisor/plugins/dns.py::_write_config`, ref `6556811`, checked 2026-11-02).
`GET /dns/info` returns `data.servers`, `data.locals` and `data.fallback`; the device's own LAN IPs come from
`GET /network/info` (`data.interfaces[].ipv4.address` / `.ipv6.address`, CIDR-suffixed strings, v1 shape; the v2 shape
nests them under `state`/`config` instead). If the device's DNS servers include the device's own IP, the device resolves
through whatever app serves :53 on it – uninstalling that app (e.g. a locally installed hickory-dns) cuts the
supervisor's own DNS off mid-task, so subsequent registry downloads fail.

Setting a host DNS server equal to the CoreDNS plugin's own address (`GET /dns/info` `data.host`, `172.30.32.3` on
standard installs) is fatal: CoreDNS's loop probe detects the self-loop and the container exits (CoreDNS log
`plugin/loop: Loop` → exit 1). The supervisor raises the `dns_loop` issue and rewrites the config dropping both
`servers` and `locals` (fallback-DoT-only config, `supervisor/plugins/dns.py::_write_config`, ref `6556811`), but the
watchdog does not reliably revive the dead container – observed on-device 2026-11-12, where it stayed dead across two
network reconfigurations until `ha dns restart`. Since `locals` always mirrors the host's NetworkManager nameservers,
the CoreDNS plugin can therefore never be the host's own resolver. Recovery order after such an outage: restore the host
DNS servers (`ha network update <iface> --ipv4-method auto --ipv4-nameserver <ip>…`; omitting `--ipv4-method` defaults
the update to static method `manual`, which NetworkManager rejects for an address-less profile), then `ha dns restart`.

The same mirroring also blocks on-device image builds (`deploy:local`) on devices whose only working plaintext resolver
is the device itself: the buildkit CLI container resolves the registry through a copy of the host's `resolv.conf`, and a
host-networked resolver answers container-sourced UDP queries with the egress route's gateway address as source IP
(per-route source selection), which DNS clients discard as source-mismatched – the build fails at
`load metadata for <base image>` before any `RUN` step runs. Substituting `172.30.32.3` as the host resolver triggers
the loop death above instead. Such devices can only take registry-deployed images (`deploy:registry`).

### Hotplug behavior

Drives are granted device access dynamically by the supervisor – including when re-attached later, without an app
restart. A drive that is detached when the app starts is passed to hd-idle for runtime resolution (by-id symlinks are
re-resolved once the drive appears) – and hd-idle applies its configured idle time to it immediately upon resolution,
without waiting for a configuration restart. The app also periodically re-resolves its configured drives: after moving
drives between ports or machines – which changes their kernel names (`/dev/sda`, `/dev/sdb`, ...) – hd-idle is restarted
automatically with the updated configuration (within about half a minute); no manual restart is needed.

## Activity log and debugging

Spin-down/spin-up events always appear in the app log. **Debug mode** adds a per-monitoring-cycle state dump for every
disk (useful when drives refuse to spin down); **Activity log** writes per-drive run/standby records to
`/data/hd-idle.log` – both field descriptions in the options UI have the details.
